How to Get Rid of Old Decking

Whether your porch board is warped, splintered, or simply past its prime, getting rid of old decking can feel like a big job. Luckily, you don’t have to tackle it alone. In this guide we’ll walk you through practical DIY steps, eco‑friendly disposal options, and when it makes sense to call in the experts—like 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK?—to take the stress out of the process.

Why Remove Old Decking?

Safety First

Rotted or loose boards can create tripping hazards and may even collapse under weight. Removing them before they become a liability protects your family and any guests.

Boost Curb Appeal

A fresh deck instantly elevates the look of your home. Getting rid of the eyesore paves the way for a new, stylish outdoor space that adds value to your property.

Prevent Pest Infestations

Stagnant wood is a favorite nesting spot for termites, carpenter ants, and rodents. By clearing out old decking, you cut off a major food source for these pests.

Options for Getting Rid of Old Decking

1. Donate Reusable Boards

If some of the lumber is still sound, consider donating it to local Habitat for Humanity ReStores, community gardens, or DIY hobbyists. A quick call or email can turn a pile of wood into a charitable contribution.

2. Recycle at a Wood Processing Facility

Many municipalities have wood recycling centers that turn old lumber into mulch, particle board, or bio‑fuel. Check your city’s waste‑management website for drop‑off locations and any fees.

3. Landfill Disposal

When the wood is beyond repair, landfill disposal is the last resort. It’s straightforward but often the most expensive option because you’ll need a dumpster or bulk‑trash pickup.

4. Hire a Junk Removal Service

Step‑by‑Step DIY Removal

Gather the Right Tools

  • Safety goggles and work gloves
  • Heavy‑duty pry bar
  • Circular saw or reciprocating saw (for cutting large sections)
  • Wheelbarrow or sturdy cart
  • Tarps to protect the ground

1. Secure the Area

Clear the space around the deck of furniture, plants, and loose items. If you’re working near a house, protect windows and siding with drop cloths.

2. Remove Fasteners

Use a pry bar or a screwdriver to pull out nails, screws, and brackets. For stubborn fasteners, a reciprocating saw with a metal blade can cut through quickly.

3. Dismantle Board by Board

Start at one corner and work your way outward. If a board is too heavy to lift, cut it into manageable lengths (about 4‑6 feet) with a circular saw. This reduces strain and speeds up loading.

4. Load the Debris

Place cut sections onto a wheelbarrow or directly onto a tarp. Stack them neatly to maximize space, especially if you’re renting a dumpster for the job.

5. Clean Up

Sweep away nails and small fragments. A magnet on a stick can help collect stray metal pieces that could be hazardous later.

6. Dispose or Recycle

When to Call the Professionals

Large‑Scale Projects

If you’re dealing with a full‑size deck (30+ square meters) or multiple structures, the amount of labor and equipment required can be overwhelming. Professionals have trucks, lifts, and crew members to finish the job quickly.

Limited Physical Ability

Removing decking is heavy work—boards can weigh 20‑30 pounds each, and you’ll be handling many of them. If back problems, arthritis, or other health concerns limit your capacity, a service like 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK? is a safe alternative.

Time Constraints

Planning a home renovation, selling a property, or prepping for an event may leave you with a tight timeline. Junk haulers can usually arrive within 24‑48 hours, making fast turnarounds possible.

Compliance with Local Regulations

Some cities require permits for deck demolition or have strict rules about wood disposal. A professional removal company knows the paperwork and can ensure you stay compliant.

Tips for Eco‑Friendly Deck Disposal

  • Separate wood from metal. Nails, screws, and brackets can be recycled separately, reducing contamination.
  • Ask about recycling. Many junk services, including 1-800‑GOT‑JUNK?, partner with recycling facilities to divert wood from landfills.
  • Consider upcycling. Creative homeowners turn old decking into garden planters, compost bins, or outdoor furniture.
  • Minimize waste. Only remove the wood you truly need to discard. Reusing as many boards as possible lessens the environmental impact.

Final Thoughts

Getting rid of old decking doesn’t have to be a daunting chore. By following the DIY steps above, you can safely dismantle your deck, recycle usable wood, and responsibly dispose of the rest.
